thread.title: Rob Arnott on Beating Stock Indexes

author: Crystal Kim
title: Rob Arnott on Beating Stock Indexes
text:
Photo: Dan Monick By Crystal Kim June 2, 2018 The modern-day Socrates wears a pinstripe suit. Rob Arnott, founder of Research Affiliates, has built a business prodding the indexing community out of complacency. And, just like the father of Western philosophy who proclaimed that he was a gadfly—irritating and easy to swat—Arnott has changed the way people think.
Arnott first made waves in the aftermath of the dot-com bubble, when he launched his firm and began to develop indexes. This, perhaps, doesn’t seem as revolutionary today as it did 15 years ago, when stock and bond indexes were virtually all structured in the same way—the largest companies held the biggest positions in them. Arnott created fundamental indexes structured around factors such as sales and dividends, rather than size. He also popularized the much-hated but never-improved-upon term “smart beta,” which refers to indexes designed not to mimic the market (or “beta”), but to beat it—a thought once the antithesis of index investing.
Now more than $730 billion is in smart-beta products, $180 billion of it in funds that have licensed Research Affiliates Fundamental Indexes—including some offered by Pimco, Invesco, and Charles Schwab.
Arnott the gadfly and his team continue to sting the industry, questioning index orthodoxy in their “Buy High, Sell Low with Index Funds.” Their new research suggests index-fund managers are willfully ignoring low-hanging alpha—the ability to beat the market—in order to slavishly hew as closely as they can to the capitalization-weighted indexes they track. Studying S&P 500 index data from 1989 to 2017, Arnott found that the stocks added to the index underperformed those that were kicked out by an average of 23 percentage points over the next 12 months. Based on that, Arnott thinks index-fund managers can do better by going after overlooked alpha. He sat down with Barron’s to explain how: lazy trading, and kicking out the biggest stock in the S&P, Apple .
Newsletter Sign-up Barron’s: Your latest research says investors who believe the market is efficient and own market capitalization-weighted portfolios end up buying high and selling low. How is that?
Rob Arnott: Indexes move stock prices when they add or remove a stock, or when they allocate more or less to a stock. Stocks added are almost always trading at high multiples. Discretionary deletions, when companies are removed for not meeting criteria, are almost always trading at bargain-bin prices. It occurred to me that no one had taken a close look at the “buy high, sell low” nature of indexes, exploring that as trading cost.
By studying historical S&P 500 index data you found the stocks added to the index underperformed the market and that the deletions outperformed in the next 12 months. Your solution is that index-fund managers should…be more active?
The point of the paper isn’t that indexing is bad, just that you can index better. It is an exploration of micro strategies, to lightly enhance returns. I’m challenging the premise that tracking error [the difference between the price of the index and that of its components] is so important that if you ignore it, you miss the easiest little bits of alpha to pick up. It’s the old joke: A person walks down a street with Eugene Fama [a Nobel-winning economist known for the Efficient Market Hypothesis]. The person sees $100 and picks it up, then asks Gene, “Why didn’t you pick it up?’ Gene goes: “Well, the market’s efficient. If that $100 is really there, it would’ve been picked up a long time ago.” Indexers are so obsessed with tracking error, they won’t seek these micro alphas.
So how would index-fund managers capture that?
Be lazy. Trade months later.
Do you mean trade months later, following an index rebalance? Please explain.
Before 1989, indexers routinely tracked reasonably closely, but underperformed slightly. Then, the S&P committee changed its rules, introducing a grace period [before indexers’ portfolios had to match the actual index]—a significant moment. So after 1989, index managers were able to make that small lag disappear by pulling the indexes down to match the funds.
That, of course, gave hedge funds the opportunity to buy the S&P and short-sell the stocks that were being deleted. Indexers move a stock enough that the entire movement is reversed in the subsequent year. So why not be lazy when the S&P indexing committee makes a change? Why not put a Post-It note three months, six months from now, and just trade then? Our simulated indexes did just that, and added decent incremental returns.
So, you’re saying smart index-fund managers would, by waiting, buy the new stock additions at a lower cost and sell deletions at a higher price.
It isn’t an existential challenge. Indexing isn’t going away. The paper isn’t triggering any overt hostility like when I introduced the first RAFI [smart beta] index. One fella who had been head of indexing activity for one of the world’s largest indexers told me that he and his team had pursued several strategies and sought to add about 10 basis points [0.10%] annually with about 15 basis points of tracking error. After several years of this, the marketing team went over to them and said, “Stop it. We’re losing to the competition.”
The competition for what?
The indexing industry did such a good job educating clients that tracking error is symptomatic of sloppiness and incompetence that even a deliberate effort to add a little bit of value for a little bit of tracking error is overtly shut down.
How widespread are your findings—does this hold for indexes besides the S&P 500?
We’ve also done this on the Russell 1000, again using a replication method. It isn’t in the early drafts of the paper, but we get similar results.
Will we see enhanced indexes from Research Affiliates?
That isn’t a business I intend to pursue. I’m much more interested in finding 100 to 200 basis points [1%-2%] of alpha for 2% to 3% of tracking error. But index-fund managers who carve out a niche as intelligent indexers, exploiting the inefficiencies created by their compatriots, could gain an edge.
It seems especially relevant now, given that stock returns aren’t likely to be nearly as robust in the next 10 years as they were in the past decade.
Exactly.
You have another suggestion for index managers: Kick out the biggest stock in the index.
Yeah, they’re not going to do that. Can you imagine someone running an MSCI ACWI index and leaving Apple out? It isn’t going to happen. The No. 1 stock is popular, beloved, and everyone thinks it deserves a lofty valuation.
But?
We simulated what would happen if you left these stocks out altogether. On average, over time, you’re only [changing the global index makeup by] 2%.
Is there anything the index providers themselves can or should do to improve?
Yes. Let’s say you’re running the Russell 1000. A stock is coming onto the list, because it just bubbled up to rank 998. There’s a chance it’ll be out the next year. Rather than risk that, why not wait until the stock is at least 40% larger than the No. 1000 company? Before you delete a stock from the list, why not wait until it’s at least 40% smaller? Doing this would reduce turnover, reduce risk, and improve performance—a trifecta.
Research Affiliates recently introduced an index that weighs stocks based on environmental, social, and governance factors, in addition to the usual fundamental metrics. Why ESG, and why now?
We aren’t getting into any area unless we think the broad market is doing it mostly wrong and that we can do it better. When it comes to environmental and social issues, my hypothesis is there is no alpha there. But governance and diversity offer alpha. You get alpha from more women in leadership and fundamental indexing. If you’ve got a crowded space—and ESG is crowded—the last thing we want to do is launch a “me-too” product.
What’s your best investment idea for the next 12 months?
Between now and mid-2019, deep-value emerging-market stocks. They present a very interesting opportunity on multiple levels. First, the pricing is cheap compared with the U.S. U.S. stocks have a Shiller price/earnings ratio between 32 and 33. Emerging market stocks are between 16 and 17. That’s half off. Historically, the average discount has been about 20%. It makes sense in that anything that is cheap is cheap for a reason, and that reason almost always has some merit, but markets are pricing in a pretty bad scenario. All it has to be is a little better for valuations to soar. The other opportunity is the growth versus value spread—it’s much wider in emerging markets than anywhere else, and it is near the widest ever. That means low-valuation stocks are trading at a deep discount to that market. Case in point: The RAFI index for emerging markets is trading less than 10 times its 10-year average earnings.
What do you think about U.S. stocks?
People buy U.S. stocks based on a presumption that things are going along smoothly and will go along smoothly forever. That could happen, but it’s also in the price. If valuations stay right where they are, 10 years from now, if you’re still at a Shiller P/E of 32, you would have collected roughly 1% growth in earnings, plus dividends. That’ll get you a 2.8% real return, pretty lousy.
If there’s any mean reversion, watch out. Historic norms for the Shiller P/E would take you from a 3% real return to minus 3%. Assuming halfway mean reversion would leave stocks at a 24 Shiller P/E, still high by historical standards, but the real return shrinks to roughly zero. That’s where we are now. Stocks are priced to offer a small risk premium over bonds if valuation levels hold, and a negative risk premium to bonds if they don’t.
Dare we ask about the FANGs?
The most popular and beloved stocks are always justified by the argument “it’s different this time.” Seven of the eight largest companies in the world as of March 31 are tech darlings Apple (ticker: AAPL), Alphabet (GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Facebook (FB), Microsoft (MSFT), Tencent (700.Hong Kong), and Alibaba (BABA). They are trading at lofty multiples, as if everything is going to be just fine. Some of these compete against each other, so the likelihood of them all succeeding is limited.
History tells us that of the top 10 stocks in the world, eight will disappear over the next decade—if history is any guide Apple might be in the Top 10, but won’t be No. 1. That means it would underperform the market. The rest will fall off the list. So if your investment horizon is 10 years, those top stocks have about a 90% chance each of underperforming. Why would you want that?
Thank you, Rob.
Corrections & Amplifications: An earlier version of this interview incorrectly stated that Arnott created the term smart beta. Consulting firm Towers Watson coined the term.
